content: CD36, also referred to as platelet glycoprotein 4, fatty acid translocase (FAT), scavenger receptor class B member 3 (SCARB3), glycoprotein 88 (GP88), glycoprotein IIIb (GPIIIb), or glycoprotein IV (GPIV), is a protein encoded by the CD36 gene in humans. This protein is an integral membrane protein expressed on the surface of various cell types in vertebrates. It plays a critical role in the uptake of fatty acids into cells and is a member of the class B scavenger receptor family of cell surface proteins. CD36 interacts with a wide range of ligands, including collagen, thrombospondin, Plasmodium falciparum-parasitized erythrocytes, oxidized low-density lipoprotein (oxLDL), native lipoproteins, oxidized phospholipids, and long-chain fatty acids. Studies in genetically modified rodents suggest that CD36 is involved in fatty acid metabolism, cardiovascular disease, taste perception, and the processing of dietary fats in the intestine. It has also been implicated in glucose intolerance, atherosclerosis, arterial hypertension, diabetes, cardiomyopathy, and Alzheimer’s disease. Structure Primary Structure In humans, rats, and mice, CD36 consists of 472 amino acids with a predicted molecular weight of approximately 53,000 Da. However, due to extensive glycosylation, its apparent molecular weight is around 88,000 Da, as determined by SDS-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis. Tertiary Structure Analysis of the CD36 amino acid sequence predicts hydrophobic regions near both ends of the protein, which are large enough to span cellular membranes. Based on this and its localization on the cell surface, CD36 is thought to adopt a hairpin-like structure, with α-helices at the Cand N-termini traversing the membrane and a large extracellular loop. This topology is supported by transfection experiments using deletion mutants of CD36. A model of the extracellular domain, based on the crystal structure of the homologous SCARB2, suggests that CD36 contains an antiparallel β-barrel core adorned with short α-helices and a hydrophobic transport tunnel. Disulfide linkages between four of the six cysteine residues in the extracellular loop are essential for efficient intracellular processing and transport of CD36 to the plasma membrane, though their role in the mature protein's function remains unclear. Posttranslational Modifications In addition to glycosylation, CD36 undergoes other posttranslational modifications. It is modified with four palmitoyl chains, two on each intracellular domain. These lipid modifications likely promote the association of CD36 with the membrane and lipid rafts, which are important for some of its functions. CD36 can also be phosphorylated at Y62, T92, and T323, ubiquitinated at K56, K469, and K472, and acetylated at K52, K56, K166, K231, K394, K398, and K403. Protein-Protein Interactions In the absence of a ligand, membrane-bound CD36 primarily exists in a monomeric state. However, upon exposure to thrombospondin, CD36 dimerizes, a process thought to play a significant role in signal transduction. Gene Structure The CD36 gene is encoded by 15 exons spanning over 32 kilobases. Both the 5' and 3' untranslated regions contain introns. Exons 1, 2, and part of exon 3, as well as exon 15, are non-coding. The N-terminal cytoplasmic and transmembrane domains are encoded by exon 3, while the C-terminal cytoplasmic and transmembrane regions are encoded by exon 14. The extracellular domain is encoded by the central 11 exons. Alternative splicing of the untranslated regions gives rise to at least two mRNA species. The transcription initiation site is located 289 nucleotides upstream of the translational start codon, with a TATA box and several putative cis-regulatory regions further upstream. A binding site for PEBP2/CBF factors has been identified between -158 and -90, and disruption of this site reduces expression. The gene is under the transcriptional control of the nuclear receptor PPAR/RXR heterodimer, and its expression can be upregulated by synthetic and natural ligands for PPAR and RXR, including thiazolidinedione anti-diabetic drugs and the vitamin A metabolite 9-cis-retinoic acid. Tissue Distribution CD36 is expressed on platelets, erythrocytes, monocytes, differentiated adipocytes, skeletal muscle, mammary epithelial cells, spleen cells, and certain skin microdermal endothelial cells. Function CD36 belongs to the class B scavenger receptor family, which includes receptors involved in selective cholesteryl ester uptake, such as scavenger receptor class B type I (SR-BI) and lysosomal integral membrane protein II (LIMP-II). CD36 interacts with various ligands, including collagen types I and IV, thrombospondin, Plasmodium falciparum-parasitized erythrocytes, platelet-agglutinating protein p37, oxidized low-density lipoprotein, and long-chain fatty acids. On macrophages, CD36 forms part of a non-opsonic receptor complex (CD36/αVβ3) involved in phagocytosis. CD36 has also been implicated in hemostasis, thrombosis, malaria, inflammation, lipid metabolism, and atherogenesis. Upon ligand binding, CD36 and its ligand are internalized via an actin-dependent mechanism requiring activation of Src-family kinases, JNK, and Rho-family GTPases. This process is independent of macropinocytosis and unaffected by inhibitors of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase or Na+/H+ exchange. CD36 ligands have also been shown to promote sterile inflammation through the assembly of a Toll-like receptor 4 and 6 heterodimer. Clinical Significance Malaria CD36 is a major sequestration receptor on microvascular endothelial cells for erythrocytes infected with mature forms of Plasmodium falciparum. Mutations in the CD36 gene, particularly in exon 5, reduce the risk of severe malaria. Gene diversity studies suggest positive selection on this gene due to malarial selection pressure. However, dissenting reports suggest that CD36 is not the sole determinant of severe malaria. CD36 also plays a role in the clearance of gametocytes and the innate immune response to malaria in mouse models. CD36 Deficiency and Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia CD36 deficiency, also known as glycoprotein IV (gpIV) or glycoprotein IIIb (gpIIIb) deficiency, is associated with the Naka antigen. It is asymptomatic in most cases but can cause refractoriness to platelet transfusion and post-transfusion purpura. CD36 deficiency is more common in certain populations, such as Japanese and sub-Saharan Africans, compared to Caucasians. Blood Pressure Reduced CD36 expression in the kidneys has been implicated as a genetic risk factor for hypertension. Fatty Acid Uptake CD36 is associated with myocardial fatty acid uptake in humans. A potential link between CD36 and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy has been suggested but requires further confirmation. Tuberculosis RNAi screening in a Drosophila model has revealed that a member of the CD36 family is required for the phagocytosis of Mycobacterium tuberculosis into macrophage phagosomes. Obesity CD36 is associated with the ability to taste fats, making it a target for studies on obesity and lipid tasting. Reduced CD36 mRNA expression in taste bud cells of obese rats suggests a link between CD36 and obesity. Altered calcium signaling in CD36-expressing taste bud cells of obese mice may contribute to decreased lipid taste sensitivity and attraction to fats. Cellular Senescence Upregulation of CD36 may contribute to membrane remodeling during senescence. CD36 stimulates NF-κB-dependent inflammatory cytokine and chemokine production, a phenomenon known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), leading to a comprehensive senescent cell fate. Cancer CD36 plays a role in angiogenesis regulation, which may be a therapeutic target for controlling cancer spread. Fatty acid uptake through CD36 may promote cancer cell migration and proliferation in hepatocellular carcinoma, glioblastoma, and potentially other cancers. Interactions CD36 has been shown to interact with FYN, a member of the Src family of tyrosine kinases. Related Proteins Other human scavenger receptors related to CD36 include SCARB1 and SCARB2 proteins.
